title: DDIA 7 · TRANSACTIONS
subtitle: A transaction groups reads and writes into one unit: all of it happens or none of it does, and concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work.
footer: Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.

head: Letter
Common belief
What it actually guarantees
rows: Abortability: on any error mid-transaction, all writes are rolled back. Safe to retry.
Committed data survives crashes (WAL + fsync, or replication). Nothing is 100%.

blocks.text: Postgres defaults to Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read.
Read committed prevents dirty reads (readers see the last committed value) and dirty writes (row locks until commit). It is the Postgres default.
Snapshot isolation: each transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start.
Optimistic (CAS): a version column; if 0 rows are updated, retry. Good under low contention. Postgres Repeatable Read also auto-detects lost updates and aborts.
Fixes: lock the rows you checked; use SERIALIZABLE; add a unique constraint; or materialize the conflict by creating a row per seat or room-night so there is something to lock.
SSI: everyone runs on snapshots without blocking. At commit, the DB checks whether anything you read has since changed and, if so, aborts you. Fast at low contention.

items: "Two users book the last room at the same time."
Write skew. Use a row per room-night + conditional UPDATE, or SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a unique constraint on (room, date).
Not row locks. Use atomic INCR in Redis, sharded counters, or batch into the DB asynchronously.
Low contention: optimistic version check. High contention on few rows (hot seat map): pessimistic lock or a queue to serialize.
No distributed ACID. Use a saga with compensations plus the outbox pattern (Ch 9 and 12).
